messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 54, Nabil is a single Middle Eastern American man who has spent most of his adult life working as a software engineer, a profession that once suited his preference for order, concentration, and long hours of solitary problem-solving. The event he speaks about in treatment happened years ago, but he recounts it with a precision that makes clear how present it still feels. He had been alone in a setting where he was suddenly with another man and quickly understood that he was not safe. What remains most vivid to him is not only the assault itself, but the atmosphere around it: the nearby sounds of emergency vehicles in the distance, the sense of being trapped in a place he could not simply leave, and the feeling of facing someone physically close to him with no help available. When he describes it, he returns again and again to the fact that it was “deeply unfair,” that he did not deserve what happened, and that nothing meaningful was ever done about it. That unfinished quality has stayed with him as strongly as the memory of the assault.

In the aftermath, Nabil found himself replaying details of his own behavior before the assault, scrutinizing small choices and wondering whether he should have spoken differently, left earlier, or recognized danger sooner. He had come to believe that the event happened because of the way he acted, and although another part of him knows this is not how he would judge someone else, the self-blame remains stubborn and immediate. He speaks about this with a kind of exhausted certainty, as if he has already prosecuted and convicted himself many times over. Alongside that is another fear that feels just as final to him: that whatever part of him used to feel ease, warmth, or ordinary emotion has been damaged beyond repair. He says he can still think clearly, still write code, still get through the day, but he no longer trusts himself to feel normal emotions in a normal way.

Over the years his world has become smaller and more tightly managed. He avoids going anywhere near the place where the assault happened, arranging routes through the city so carefully that what looks to others like inconvenience feels to him like basic survival. He does the same with people who represent authority. Police officers, military uniforms, visible weapons, even the sight of someone dressed in a way that suggests official power can make his body tense before he has fully registered why. He does not experience these reactions as exaggerated. In those moments he feels as though danger is already underway, and he reacts accordingly. He also tries hard not to find himself alone with men. In professional settings he keeps interactions brief and bounded when possible, preferring group meetings, open doors, and remote communication. Working in software has allowed some accommodation; he can spend long stretches at a screen, message colleagues instead of walking over, and structure his day around predictability. Even so, the office still presents moments he cannot fully control. If a male coworker lingers in a conference room after others leave, Nabil feels his attention sharpen instantly. He begins scanning the exits, the other man’s posture, the hallway beyond the glass. He knows on one level that this is a meeting at work, not the assault, but his body does not wait for that conclusion.

Sirens are especially potent. If an ambulance passes his apartment or cuts through traffic while he is driving, he feels a jolt that seems to erase the present for a second. He becomes intensely alert, looking around for who is near him, where authority figures might appear, whether he can get home quickly. Ambulances do not register for him as neutral signs of emergency services; they bring back the entire emotional climate of vulnerability and threat. Because of this, he has narrowed the places where he feels safe to a very limited set of environments, mainly his apartment and a few highly familiar locations he can enter and leave on his own terms. Outside those places he is constantly scanning, measuring distance, checking who is behind him, who is in front of him, and whether anyone in uniform is nearby.

This pattern has altered his life in concrete ways. He has turned down in-person work events, left gatherings early when he noticed police presence nearby, and rerouted his commute to avoid parts of the city associated with the assault. Colleagues know him as capable but withdrawn. He has remained single, and while he does not present this simply as a symptom, he acknowledges that being close to others, especially men in unstructured settings, feels almost impossible. What finally brought him to seek help was the growing sense that his life had become organized around anticipating danger and injustice, with too little room left for anything else. He was alarmed by how quickly he still reacted as if he were in immediate peril when nothing observable was wrong. Sitting in the consulting room, he said that what frightened him most was not only that the past still had this kind of force, but that he might never feel normal emotions again. At the same time, he is coming to treatment because he wants some part of his life back—more than just functioning, he wants the possibility of feeling safe somewhere beyond the few places he can currently tolerate.
